summary: At Judah's urging Jacob shoots and kills Esau, and Jacob's sons attack the allied forces from four sides of the tower. Jacob buries his brother while his sons pursue the survivors to Seir, where they impose peace through tribute and servitude; a list of Edom's kings closes the chapter.
whyItMatters: The story resolves the renewed fraternal conflict through Esau's death and the subordination of his descendants. Burial and peace do not undo the violence or the unequal settlement the chapter describes.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: Jacob's tower and its surrounding battlefield, the hill of Aduram where Esau is buried, and the mountains of Seir.
context.literaryForm: Battle narrative, imposed peace and tribute notice, followed by a royal succession list.

before.text: Esau has rejected his oath and any future peace, and Jacob has ordered his household to attack.

here.text: The battle's decisive act is Jacob's killing of his own brother, followed by pursuit and a choice to impose servitude on the survivors.

after.text: The narrative returns to Joseph in Egypt, where his entrusted position in a master's household gives way to coercion and imprisonment.

outline.heading: Jacob kills Esau and Adoran
outline.note: Judah urges Jacob to shoot the enemy, and Jacob kills his brother and an allied leader.

outline.heading: Four companies attack
outline.note: Jacob’s sons and servants strike the allied forces on each side of the tower.

outline.heading: Pursuit and Esau’s burial
outline.note: Jacob buries Esau while his sons pursue and subdue the survivors in Seir.

outline.heading: Peace under servitude
outline.note: Jacob chooses peace over further killing, but the agreement requires tribute and a continuing yoke.

outline.heading: The kings of Edom
outline.note: A succession list records rulers, origins, cities, and one royal marriage.

keyVerses.text: Then Jacob bent his bow and sent forth the arrow and struck Esau, his brother (on his right breast) and slew him.
keyVerses.why: The text directly attributes Esau’s death to Jacob, rather than to an unnamed warrior.

keyVerses.text: And Jacob sent word to his sons that they should make peace, and they made peace with them, and placed the yoke of servitude upon them, so that they paid tribute to Jacob and to his sons always.
keyVerses.why: The peace Jacob orders is explicitly a settlement of servitude and tribute.

keyVerses.text: And the sons of Edom have not got quit of the yoke of servitude which the twelve sons of Jacob had imposed on them until this day.
keyVerses.why: The narrator extends the story’s claim of Edomite subordination to its own “until this day.”

questions.question: Who kills Esau?
questions.answer: Jacob himself shoots the fatal arrow after Judah urges him to do so. The account is explicit about the brother killing his brother and should not be retold as a death by an unidentified soldier.

questions.question: Why does Judah call it an “honour” to leave Esau to Jacob?
questions.answer: Judah says the sons will not kill their father's brother because he is like Jacob and should receive that honor. The disturbing result is that the supposed honor assigns the killing to Jacob rather than sparing Esau.

questions.question: How is the attack organized?
questions.answer: The sons and servants divide into companies on all four sides of the tower, with different family members named in each group. The arrangement emphasizes coordinated victory over the coalition described in the preceding chapter.

questions.question: Does Jacob leave Esau unburied?
questions.answer: No. While his sons pursue the fugitives, Jacob buries his brother on the hill where he fell and then returns home. The burial acknowledges the dead brother within a story that has already made reconciliation impossible.

questions.question: What does the “yoke of servitude” mean?
questions.answer: It describes the subordination imposed on Esau's surviving descendants, expressed in tribute to Jacob and his sons. The metaphor makes clear that the peace is constrained by the victor's authority.

questions.question: What does “until this day” establish?
questions.answer: It marks the narrator's claim that the subordination continues into the account's own present. By itself the phrase does not identify a modern date or independently prove the historical duration of the tribute.

questions.question: Why end with a list of Edom’s kings?
questions.answer: The list shifts from the battle between ancestors to the succession of rulers associated with Edom. It supplies names and places without explaining how every reign relates chronologically to the preceding account of tribute.

glossary.def: Payments demanded from the defeated descendants of Esau as part of their subordination.
The image for the authority Jacob’s sons impose on the survivors in Seir.
The repeated phrase marking one king’s replacement by the next in Edom’s royal list.
